16990:
To veer means to suddenly change direction — to shift away from the path, course, or direction you were on before.

The single most important thing to understand about "veer" is that the change is noticeable and fairly sharp. It is not a slow, gradual drift. Something that veers makes a clear, definite turn away from where it was headed.

1. Literal / Physical Meaning

This is when something that is moving changes its physical direction.

  • A car driving straight on the highway suddenly veers to the right.
  • A cyclist loses control and veers off the road.
  • A football is kicked toward the goal, but it veers left at the last second.
  • A plane veers away from a storm cloud.

In all these cases, something is moving in one direction — and then, quite suddenly, it goes a different way. The original path is abandoned.

Key feel: You can almost see the sharp change happening. It has a sense of urgency or abruptness to it.

2. Figurative / Abstract Meaning

This is where "veer" gets really useful. You can use it for things that don't physically move but that change their direction in a broader sense — like a conversation, a story, a person's behavior, a country's politics, or a mood.

  • A friendly conversation veers into an argument nobody wanted.
  • A comedy film suddenly veers toward dark, serious territory.
  • His speech was about the economy, but it kept veering off topic.
  • The country began to veer toward authoritarianism.
  • She was calm, then her mood veered sharply to anger.

Here, the "direction" is not physical — it's the direction of a situation, idea, or tone. But the feeling is the same: there was a clear path being followed, and then — a sudden, notable shift away from it.
What "Veer" Feels Like vs. Similar Words

Understanding a word fully means knowing what makes it different from its neighbors.

Veer vs. Turn
"Turn" is neutral and planned. You turn left at a traffic light — that's expected. But if your car veers left, that feels unintended, sharp, and possibly alarming. Veer carries a sense of deviation — something moving away from where it was supposed to go.

Veer vs. Swerve
These are very close. Both suggest a sharp, sudden change. But "swerve" tends to suggest a reactive movement — you swerve to avoid something (a pothole, a cat). "Veer" is a bit broader and doesn't always imply a specific thing being avoided. You can veer simply because of wind, loss of control, or a change in intention.

Veer vs. Drift
"Drift" is slow and gradual — like a boat slowly drifting off course over time without anyone noticing right away. "Veer" is more sudden and obvious. If a conversation drifts off topic, it happens quietly. If it veers off topic, the shift is more noticeable and sharp.

Veer vs. Deviate
"Deviate" is more formal and clinical — used in technical or serious contexts (a plane deviates from its flight plan). "Veer" is more vivid and dynamic; it paints a picture in your mind of actual movement happening.

"Veer" often carries a mild sense that the change was not fully in control, not perfectly planned, or not entirely welcome. When something veers, there's usually a sense that it was heading one way — and then, for whatever reason (an obstacle, a force, a decision, an emotion), it went another way instead.

This is why "veer" often appears in situations with a slight edge of tension, surprise, or concern:

  • "The car suddenly veered toward the barrier." (alarming)
  • "The debate veered into personal insults." (unwanted)
  • "Her career unexpectedly veered away from medicine." (surprising)

However, it is not always negative. Sometimes a veer is simply interesting or unexpected:

  • "The documentary veers between heartbreak and humor." (describes tonal shifts)
  • "The trail veers right at the big oak tree." (simple directions)

Notice the prepositions that follow "veer" most naturally:

  • veer off — veer off the road, veer off course, veer off topic (moving away from something)
  • veer toward / towards — veer toward chaos, veer toward the left (moving in the direction of something)
  • veer away from — veer away from tradition, veer away from the truth (moving in the opposite direction from something)
  • veer into — veer into dangerous territory, veer into comedy (entering a new space or zone)
  • veer left / right — a simple directional shift

If you had to remember one sentence for the rest of your life about what "veer" means, let it be this:

To veer is to suddenly shift away from the direction, course, or path you were on — whether you're a car on a road, a story in a book, a conversation between friends, or a country in history.

The change is noticeable. It's fairly sharp. And it usually carries the feeling that something has departed from what was expected or established before.
16991:
When something is described as vegan, it means it involves no animal products whatsoever — not in its ingredients, not in its making, and not in what it comes from.

The word applies to food, products, and people. Think of it as a strict filter: if anything from an animal touched it, it is not vegan.

This is the key to understanding the word deeply. An animal product is anything that comes from an animal's body — whether the animal was killed for it or not. This includes:

  • Meat of any kind: beef, pork, chicken, fish, seafood, and even insects
  • Dairy: milk, cheese, butter, cream, yogurt, ghee
  • Eggs
  • Honey (bees are animals, and honey is what they produce)
  • Gelatin (made from boiled animal bones and skin — found in many gummies, jellies, and marshmallows)
  • Rennet (from animal stomachs, used in many cheeses)
  • Certain food dyes, like carmine — a red colour made from crushed insects (cochineal)
  • Animal-derived fats like lard (pig fat) or tallow (beef fat)

Notice that even things like milk and eggs — which don't require killing an animal — are still not vegan. This is a crucial distinction. Veganism isn't just about avoiding death; it's about avoiding all use and exploitation of animals.

When a dish, meal, or ingredient is called vegan, it means every single component came from plants, fungi, or minerals — nothing from an animal.

  • A vegan burger is made from plants (like lentils, mushrooms, or soy), not from beef. It also contains no eggs as a binder and no dairy-based cheese.
  • A vegan cake uses no eggs and no butter or milk — perhaps using coconut oil and plant-based milk instead.
  • Vegan chocolate contains no milk solids (dark chocolate is often, but not always, vegan — it depends on the recipe).
  • Vegan cheese is made from nuts, soy, or other plants, not from dairy.

A common mistake beginners make: assuming something is vegan just because it has no meat. A vegetable soup cooked in chicken broth, for instance, is not vegan, even though it contains only vegetables.

The adjective extends well beyond food. Many everyday products are made using animal materials:

  • Leather comes from animal skin (usually cow)
  • Wool comes from sheep
  • Silk comes from silkworm cocoons
  • Down (the filling in many pillows and jackets) comes from duck or goose feathers
  • Beeswax (used in lip balms, candles, and polishes) comes from bees
  • Lanolin (a common moisturiser) comes from sheep's wool
  • Many cosmetics and skincare products are tested on animals or contain animal-derived ingredients

When a product is called vegan, it means none of these are present. A vegan leather jacket is made from a synthetic or plant-based material (like polyurethane or even pineapple fibres) rather than animal skin. Vegan cosmetics contain no animal ingredients and are not tested on animals.

When a person is described as vegan (e.g. "She is vegan"), it means they have chosen a lifestyle that avoids using or consuming anything derived from animals — in their food, clothing, and often in all other areas of life (cleaning products, cosmetics, furniture, etc.).

This is a lifestyle rooted in a philosophy called veganism, which holds that animals are not ours to use — not for food, not for clothing, not for entertainment, and not for any other purpose. The motivation can be:

  • Ethical: a belief that animals can suffer and should not be exploited
  • Environmental: animal agriculture is a major contributor to greenhouse gas emissions, deforestation, and water usage
  • Health-related: some people adopt a vegan diet for perceived health benefits

These two words are often confused, but they are not the same.

A vegetarian does not eat meat (no beef, pork, chicken, or fish), but may still eat dairy products, eggs, and honey. There are several sub-types (like lacto-vegetarian, ovo-vegetarian, etc.) but the common thread is: no flesh.

A vegan goes further. A vegan avoids all animal products — including the dairy and eggs that most vegetarians still consume. So all vegans follow a vegetarian diet, but not all vegetarians are vegan.

Think of it this way:

  • Vegetarian = no animal flesh
  • Vegan = no animal products of any kind

You may sometimes hear the phrase "dietary vegan" — this refers to someone who follows a vegan diet (no animal products in food) but doesn't necessarily extend this to their clothing or other lifestyle choices. This is considered a less complete form of veganism by those who follow it strictly.

The word "vegan-friendly" is also widely used. It means something is suitable for a vegan — a restaurant might advertise "vegan-friendly options," meaning they have dishes that contain no animal products.
A quick summary to lock it in

The adjective vegan means: completely free from all animal products and by-products, whether applied to food, clothing, cosmetics, or any other thing. When applied to a person, it describes someone who avoids all animal products as a matter of principle — in what they eat, wear, and use.

It is stricter than "vegetarian," which only avoids meat. Veganism draws the line at anything that comes from an animal's body, regardless of whether the animal was harmed or killed.
16992: A vegetarian is a person who does not eat the flesh of any animal. This means they avoid beef, pork, chicken, lamb, fish, shrimp, and the meat of any other creature. Instead, they build their diet entirely around plant-based foods — vegetables, fruits, grains, legumes (like lentils and beans), nuts, and seeds.
What vegetarians eat and don't eat

This is where it gets a little nuanced, so pay attention.

The word "vegetarian" does not automatically mean someone avoids all animal products. It specifically means they avoid killing animals for food — in other words, they don't eat flesh. Because of this, most vegetarians still consume things that come from animals without killing them, such as:

  • Dairy products — milk, cheese, butter, yogurt, cream
  • Eggs — since an unfertilised egg is not a living creature

So a typical vegetarian's plate might include a cheese omelette, a glass of milk, and a vegetable curry — perfectly vegetarian, but not entirely "animal-free."

The word "vegetarian" is actually an umbrella term. Under it, there are several varieties based on exactly what a person eats or avoids:

1. Lacto-ovo vegetarian
This is the most common type, and when most people say "vegetarian" without any extra label, this is what they mean. These people eat both dairy (lacto) and eggs (ovo), but no meat of any kind.

2. Lacto vegetarian
Eats dairy products, but not eggs. Many vegetarians in India fall into this category for cultural or religious reasons.

3. Ovo vegetarian
Eats eggs, but not dairy products.

4. Vegan
A vegan takes vegetarianism to its furthest point. They avoid all animal products — no meat, no dairy, no eggs, no honey, and often no animal-derived materials (like leather or wool) in their personal lives either. Vegans are sometimes called "strict vegetarians," but today the standard word for them is simply vegan. All vegans are vegetarians, but not all vegetarians are vegans.

5. Pescatarian (important distinction)
A pescatarian avoids all meat except fish and other seafood. Despite what many people assume, pescatarians are not vegetarians in the strict sense, because fish are animals. However, in casual or cultural usage, some people mistakenly include pescatarians under the vegetarian label — especially in some parts of South Asia. If you want to be precise: eating fish disqualifies you from being called a vegetarian.

6. Flexitarian
Someone who follows a mostly vegetarian diet but occasionally eats meat. They are also not true vegetarians — the word simply doesn't apply if a person sometimes eats animal flesh.

A person can become a vegetarian for many different reasons, and two vegetarians sitting at the same table may have completely different motivations:

  • Ethical reasons — They believe it is morally wrong to kill animals for food, since animals can feel pain and suffer.
  • Environmental reasons — Raising animals for meat is resource-intensive: it uses vast amounts of land, water, and energy, and produces a large share of greenhouse gas emissions. Many people go vegetarian as an act of environmental responsibility.
  • Health reasons — Studies have consistently found that well-planned vegetarian diets are associated with lower risks of heart disease, type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, obesity, and certain types of cancer.
  • Religious or spiritual reasons — Many religions either encourage or require vegetarianism. Hinduism, Jainism, and certain schools of Buddhism emphasise non-violence towards all living beings (ahimsa in Sanskrit), which leads many of their followers to avoid meat. Some Christian denominations also practice vegetarianism.
  • Cultural reasons — In some communities, vegetarianism is simply the norm passed down through generations, unrelated to any conscious choice.
  • Dislike of meat — Some people simply find the taste, texture, or smell of meat unappealing.
  • Economic reasons — In many parts of the world, plant-based foods are cheaper than meat, making vegetarianism a practical choice for budget-conscious households.
A subtle but important point: hidden animal products

Stricter vegetarians pay attention to ingredients that most people don't think about:

  • Gelatin — found in many sweets, jellies, and marshmallows; it is made by boiling animal bones and skin.
  • Rennet — an enzyme from animal stomachs, used in producing many types of hard cheese. Some vegetarians specifically choose "vegetarian cheese" made with plant-based or microbial rennet.
  • Carmine (also called cochineal or E120) — a red food dye made from crushed insects, used in some juices, jams, and cosmetics.

Casual vegetarians may not be aware of or concerned about these; strict vegetarians actively avoid them.
How the word is used in sentences

• "She became a vegetarian at the age of sixteen after learning about factory farming."
  • "The menu has several options for vegetarians, including a lentil soup and a paneer dish."
  • "He is a vegetarian for health reasons, though he still drinks milk and eats eggs."
  • "Not all vegetarians are vegans — many still consume dairy."

A vegetarian is a person who does not eat the flesh of animals, but who may still eat other animal products like dairy and eggs depending on their personal choices. The word covers a spectrum, from those who simply avoid meat to those who avoid almost all animal-derived ingredients — with vegan representing the strictest end of that spectrum.
16993:
To vegetate means to live or spend time in a way that is dull, inactive, and mentally empty — doing very little, thinking very little, and barely engaging with life. The person is physically alive and present, but not really living in any meaningful, active sense.

The word is directly inspired by the image of a vegetable. A vegetable just sits there — it doesn't move, doesn't think, doesn't make decisions, doesn't grow in interesting directions. It simply exists. When a person vegetates, they are being compared to that vegetable. They are alive, but barely doing anything more than existing.

1. The Everyday, Informal Meaning (the most common one)

This is when a person spends their time doing nothing productive, stimulating, or engaging. They are mentally switched off — sitting around, not pursuing goals, not socializing meaningfully, not challenging their mind. It could mean lying on a couch for hours watching mindless TV, scrolling a phone without purpose, or simply doing nothing day after day.

Examples:

  • "He just vegetated at home all weekend."
  • "She felt like she was vegetating at that job — same routine, no growth, no challenge."
  • "I don't want to spend my retirement just vegetating."

Notice that in all these cases, the person isn't suffering in an obvious, dramatic way. They're just... not really living. They're going through the motions. Life is passing them by.

2. The Literal / Biological Meaning (less common, more technical)

In a more literal, scientific sense, to vegetate means to grow like a plant — to sprout, spread, or develop as vegetation does. This usage appears in biology or botany and is rarely used in everyday conversation.

Example:

  • "The seeds began to vegetate after the first rains."

Unless you are reading scientific texts, you are very unlikely to encounter this meaning in daily life.
The Tone and Feeling of the Word

This is important: vegetate carries a negative or pitying tone. It quietly judges the situation. When you say someone is vegetating, you are subtly saying their existence at that moment (or in general) is pointless, unstimulating, or beneath their potential.

However — and this is a key nuance — sometimes people use it about themselves, lightly and without shame, especially when they want to rest completely and switch off.

Example:

  • "I'm so exhausted. I just want to go home and vegetate for a few days."

Here, the person isn't being self-critical. They are saying: "I want to do absolutely nothing, and I'm okay with that — I've earned it." It becomes a way of expressing a desire for total rest. The negative edge softens when used this way.

So the tone depends on context:

  • Used about someone else, or about a long-term pattern → usually negative and judgmental.
  • Used about yourself for a short recovery period → often casual, neutral, or even slightly humorous.
What Exactly Does "Doing Nothing" Mean Here?

A person can be physically busy and still vegetate — for example, someone doing a completely brainless, repetitive task day after day with no growth, no connection, no meaning. The key thing that vegetating describes is the absence of mental and emotional engagement. The mind is idle. Life has no momentum.

It is not just about being lazy on one afternoon. It carries a sense of a lifestyle or at least a prolonged stretch of time — days, weeks, years — spent in this hollow, passionless state.

It is moderately strong — not an insult exactly, but not gentle either. It does not mean you are a bad person. It means you are wasting your potential or your time. It evokes a gentle sadness or frustration rather than anger.

• Vegetation (noun) → the plants of a region, OR the act/state of vegetating.
  • Vegetative (adjective) → relating to plant growth, OR describing a state of minimal brain activity (as in a vegetative state in medicine — a serious condition where a person is alive but has no conscious awareness).
To vegetate means to exist in a passive, mindless, and unstimulating way — mentally switched off, doing nothing meaningful — like a plant that simply sits in one place and does nothing but exist.
16994:
Vehemence is the quality of being extremely forceful, passionate, and intense — especially in the way someone feels, speaks, or acts. It describes an energy that is so strong it almost feels like it cannot be contained or held back. It bursts out.

When someone feels or expresses something with vehemence, they are not being mild, quiet, or half-hearted about it. They are going at it with full, burning force.
What Does It Actually Feel Like?

Think of a spectrum of intensity. On one end, you have someone who is slightly annoyed. In the middle, someone who is quite upset. On the far end — almost vibrating with emotion, voice loud and sharp, every word landing like a punch — that person is operating with vehemence.

It is not just "strong feeling." It is strong feeling that shows itself with force and urgency. You can sense vehemence in the air. It has a kind of heat to it.

Vehemence can colour many different things.

In speech and arguments: When someone argues a point with vehemence, they are not just saying "I disagree." They are making their case with intense conviction, raised passion, and an almost unstoppable urgency. A lawyer making a passionate closing argument, a person furiously defending an innocent friend — this is vehemence in speech.

In emotions: Anger, love, hatred, grief, enthusiasm — any of these, when felt at an extreme and burning level, can be described as being felt with vehemence. A mother fiercely defending her child is acting out of vehemence. A protester screaming for justice is speaking with vehemence.

In actions and physical force: Vehemence is not limited to words or feelings. Physical things can also carry it. A storm that hits a coastline with overwhelming, battering force has a kind of vehemence. Someone slamming a door so hard the walls shake — that action carries vehemence too.

Vehemence sits at an interesting crossroads. It is not automatically negative or positive — it depends entirely on the situation.

It can be admirable. A doctor fighting with vehemence for a patient's life, a civil rights activist speaking with vehemence for justice — here, vehemence is a good thing. It signals deep care and moral fire.

It can also suggest something excessive or unsettling. If someone reacts to a minor disagreement with vehemence — screaming, insisting, refusing to back down — the word hints that the response is disproportionate and overpowering.

In both cases, what makes it vehemence is the same: extraordinary, forceful intensity that is hard to ignore and hard to stop.

These examples will show you how the word lands in real use:

  • "She denied the accusation with such vehemence that the room fell completely silent." — Her denial was not gentle or calm. It was fierce and overwhelming.
  • "The vehemence of his opposition surprised everyone in the meeting." — Nobody expected him to push back so powerfully and with such burning force.
  • "He had argued his case with surprising vehemence, given how soft-spoken he normally was." — His usual quietness made the intensity of his passion even more striking.
  • "The protesters marched with a vehemence born of years of frustration." — Their energy was not casual. It was raw, concentrated, and impossible to dismiss.
How It Differs From Similar Words

Words like passion, intensity, fervor, force, and zeal are all cousins of vehemence, but there are real differences.

Passion is a broad word for deep feeling — it can be quiet, private, even gentle. Vehemence is specifically about that passion pushing outward with force and urgency. You can have quiet passion; you cannot have quiet vehemence.

Zeal suggests enthusiastic dedication to a cause. It feels purposeful and driven. Vehemence is more about the raw force of the feeling itself — it doesn't always need a clear purpose.

Fervor is warm and glowing intensity, often with a sense of religious or idealistic devotion. Vehemence is sharper, more explosive, more confrontational in tone.

Force is purely physical and neutral. Vehemence almost always carries emotional weight alongside the force.

So vehemence is the word you reach for when you want to capture something that is forceful, passionate, emotionally charged, and hard to ignore — all at once.

If vehemence is heat and force, its opposites are words like mildness, calmness, indifference, restraint, and passivity. A person who speaks with vehemence is the exact opposite of someone who shrugs and says, "Well, I suppose it doesn't really matter either way."
One Final Way to Remember It

If you want a mental anchor, think of it this way: vehemence is what happens when a feeling is turned up so high it refuses to stay still. It demands to be seen, heard, or felt. It has edges. It has heat. It does not whisper — it insists.
16995: Vehement describes something expressed or done with intense, forceful emotion and strong conviction — not quietly, not mildly, but with unmistakable passion and energy.

When you feel something deeply and you express it with force, urgency, and visible intensity, that expression is vehement. The word captures two things at once: the strength of the feeling inside a person, and the powerful, energetic way that feeling is shown on the outside.

Think of it this way. You can disagree with someone quietly and politely. Or you can disagree with fire — raising your voice, speaking with conviction, gesturing firmly, leaving absolutely no doubt about where you stand. The second kind of disagreement is vehement.

So vehement is not just about how much you feel something. It's also about how forcefully and openly you express it. A feeling can be deep but hidden. Vehement feelings are not hidden — they burst outward with intensity.

The defining quality of vehement is passionate intensity. This means the emotion is not calm, not controlled, not lukewarm. It is hot, driven, urgent, and powerful. When someone is vehement, you feel the weight of their conviction. There is an almost overwhelming quality to it — as if the person cannot hold back what they feel.

This is what separates vehement from just "strong." Something can be strong but restrained. Vehement is never restrained. It is always openly, actively intense.

The adjective vehement can describe many things. Here are the most common:

A person can be vehement when they speak or act with fierce passion. "She was vehement in her demands for justice."

Speech or language can be vehement when it is forceful, heated, and driven by strong feeling. "His vehement speech moved the entire crowd."

A denial or refusal can be vehement when it is not just a "no" but a fierce, energetic, unmistakable "absolutely not." "The accused gave a vehement denial of all the charges."

Opposition or protest can be vehement when it is not passive resistance but loud, driven, forceful pushback. "There was vehement opposition from the public."

An argument or disagreement can be vehement when it is not a calm debate but a heated, intense clash of strong views.

An emotion or feeling, like love, anger, or belief, can be described as vehement when it is overwhelming in its strength and urgency.

Vehement is neutral in itself — it simply describes intensity of expression. But in practice, it most often appears in contexts involving opposition, disagreement, denial, or protest. This is simply because forceful, intense expression tends to arise most naturally when people are fighting against something or defending themselves.

That said, it can absolutely appear in positive contexts. You can have a vehement supporter, a vehement declaration of love, or vehement praise. The intensity is the point, not whether the feeling is for or against something.

• The politician faced vehement criticism after his remarks.
  • She was a vehement supporter of animal rights and made that known to everyone she met.
  • Despite the evidence, he issued a vehement denial.
  • The crowd's vehement reaction surprised even the organizers.
  • He spoke with such vehement conviction that nobody dared to question him.
  • Her vehement objection stopped the plan in its tracks.
How it compares to similar words

Passionate means driven by deep feeling, but it sounds warmer and more personal. Vehement sounds more forceful and combative.

Fervent means deeply earnest and sincere. It's intense, but more inward and warm. Vehement has more outward force to it.

Fierce focuses on raw aggression and power. Vehement adds the dimension of emotional conviction — it's not just powerful, it's passionately powerful.

Adamant means absolutely refusing to change your position. Vehement means expressing that position (or any position) with intense force. You can be adamant quietly; you cannot be vehement quietly.

Emphatic means clearly and forcefully stated. It is the closest sibling of vehement, but emphatic is milder. Emphatic is a firm knock on the table; vehement is a fist slamming on it.

To understand vehement even better, consider what it is not: mild, gentle, calm, subdued, indifferent, half-hearted, lukewarm, restrained. These are all the opposites of vehement. If someone makes a mild objection, it is the direct opposite of a vehement one.
The one thing to always remember

If you ever forget the precise meaning, just remember this: vehement = intense + forceful + passionate, expressed outwardly. Whenever you see or use this word, picture someone who cannot contain the strength of what they feel, and shows it with unmistakable, heated energy. That image will never steer you wrong.
16996:
Vehemently means with great force, intense emotion, and strong conviction — in a way that is energetic, passionate, and hard to ignore.

When someone does something vehemently, they are not just expressing a feeling — they are expressing it powerfully and urgently, in a way that makes it very clear how strongly they feel.

The word carries three things at once:

  1. Intensity — the feeling is very strong, not mild or moderate
  2. Outward expression — that strong feeling comes out forcefully; it doesn't stay hidden inside
  3. Conviction — the person genuinely, deeply believes in what they are saying or doing

So "vehemently" is not just about feeling something strongly in your heart. It is about showing that strength — through your words, your tone, your body language, your actions.

Think of a courtroom scene. A defendant stands up and says, "I did NOT do this." But it's not a quiet, calm statement. His voice is firm and charged with emotion. He leans forward. He means every word with every part of himself.

That energy — that forceful, almost physical intensity of expression — is what vehemently captures.

It sits at the high end of intensity. Here's a rough scale to feel this:

  • mildly → moderately → strongly → vehemently → (almost beyond control)

It describes an expression that is at or near the peak — but still controlled and purposeful. It is not random outburst; it is focused, strong force.

Vehemently is most commonly used in contexts where someone is resisting, opposing, defending, or denying something. This is its natural home. Look at the words it most often pairs with:

  • vehemently deny — refuse to accept blame or accusation with great force
  • vehemently oppose — strongly push back against a plan or idea
  • vehemently disagree — reject someone's view with intense conviction
  • vehemently protest — speak or act against something with passion
  • vehemently object — raise a strong, charged objection
  • vehemently argue — defend a position with great energy
  • vehemently defend — protect something or someone with strong conviction
  • vehemently insist — repeat a claim with great force and certainty

Notice the pattern: vehemently almost always appears when someone is pushing back against something — an accusation, a decision, an idea, a person. It is the word of resistance done with power.

1. She vehemently denied having anything to do with the missing money.

→ She didn't just say "I didn't do it" softly. She rejected the idea with full force and emotion.

  1. The workers vehemently opposed the new policy.

→ They didn't just quietly dislike it. They pushed back against it with strong, visible conviction.

  1. He vehemently argued that the decision was unfair.

→ He made his case with great energy and passion — not calmly, but forcefully.

  1. The scientist vehemently defended her research.

→ She stood behind her work with intense commitment, refusing to back down.

  1. Critics vehemently objected to the government's plan.

→ The objection was not mild or polite — it was loud, charged, and clear.
How it differs from similar words

Several words seem close to vehemently, but each has its own flavor:

  • Strongly — general and neutral. "She strongly disagreed." This is plain force, without emotional heat. It's the most common, least colorful option.
  • Passionately — full of deep emotion. It emphasizes feeling. "He passionately argued his case." It can be used for positive things (passionately in love, passionately committed).
  • Fervently — emotional and earnest, but often carries a warm, almost hopeful quality. "She fervently prayed for peace." More about inner sincerity than outward force.
  • Fiercely — aggressive, almost combative. "He fiercely defended his territory." It suggests a kind of fighting edge.
  • Vehemently — combines forcefulness + emotional charge + visible outward expression. It is most naturally used for opposition and resistance. It suggests both the internal strength of conviction AND the external energy of expression. It's more formal and precise than "strongly," more forceful and outward-facing than "fervently," and less aggressive or combative than "fiercely."

If you want one sentence: vehemently is the word you reach for when someone expresses disagreement or resistance in a way that is charged with emotion, delivered with force, and rooted in deep conviction.

Vehemently is a formal to semi-formal word. You will see it most often in:

  • News articles: "The minister vehemently denied the allegations."
  • Books and academic writing
  • Legal or official contexts
  • Careful, articulate speech

In casual everyday conversation, people tend to say things like "she really strongly disagreed" or "he totally opposed it." Vehemently sounds educated and precise. Using it in writing or formal speech will immediately signal that you have a good command of the language.
A one-sentence summary to remember it forever

Vehemently = with great force and intense emotion, especially when opposing, denying, or defending something with deep conviction.

If you can picture someone leaning forward, voice firm and charged, refusing to back down — that is the image of vehemently in action.
16997: A veil is something that covers or hides — but not completely. This is the most important thing to understand about the word. A veil doesn't block something out entirely like a wall does. It softens it, obscures it, makes it unclear or mysterious. Think of it as a "partial hiding." Whether it's used literally or figuratively, that sense of something being there, but not fully visible or known, is almost always present.

In its most direct, physical sense, a veil is a thin piece of fabric — often sheer, lightweight, and see-through to some degree — that is worn over or in front of something, usually a person's face or head.

Common real-world examples:

  • A bridal veil is the iconic piece of soft, gauzy fabric a bride wears over her face or draped from her head on her wedding day. You can still make out her face through it, but it's softened and partially hidden — which is exactly the point.
  • Nuns in many religious traditions wear a veil over their head as a sign of devotion and modesty. It covers the hair and frames the face.
  • A beekeeper's veil is a protective mesh screen worn over the face and head to guard against bee stings. It lets the beekeeper see clearly but shields them from harm.
  • Women in certain cultures and religions wear a veil as a form of modesty or religious observance.
  • In the past, women attending funerals would wear a dark veil over their face as a symbol of grief and mourning.

In all these cases, the veil is a real thing you can touch — a fabric that sits between a person and the outside world.
The Figurative Meaning (The Far More Powerful Use)

This is where the word truly comes alive, and where you'll encounter it most often in literature, journalism, and everyday speech. When used figuratively, a veil is anything — invisible, abstract — that hides, obscures, or disguises something from being fully seen or understood.

Just as a physical veil blurs a face, a figurative veil blurs the truth, a feeling, or a reality. Here are the key ways this plays out:

1. A veil of something = a thin layer that obscures

You'll very commonly see "a veil of [something]" used to describe a thin, obscuring layer of something in nature or atmosphere:

  • "A veil of mist hung over the valley." — The mist didn't completely block the view of the valley, but it made everything hazy and unclear. You could sense the valley was there, but you couldn't see it sharply.
  • "A veil of smoke drifted through the air."
  • "The mountains were hidden behind a veil of clouds."

Notice the pattern: the thing described as a "veil" always partially obscures something, rather than blocking it entirely.

2. A veil of secrecy / silence / mystery

Here, "veil" describes something kept deliberately hidden or unknown:

  • "The project was carried out behind a veil of secrecy." — Nobody outside was allowed to know what was happening. The secrecy acted like a fabric draped over the whole thing, hiding it from public view.
  • "There was a veil of mystery surrounding her past." — Her history wasn't known; something was concealing it.
  • "He answered every question from behind a veil of lies." — His lies were what stood between the truth and the world.

3. A veil over emotions or reality

A veil can describe something that blunts or softens how clearly a person perceives reality — like grief, illness, or shock casting a haze over someone's thinking:

  • "After her loss, a veil of sadness settled over her life." — Sadness coloured and clouded everything she experienced.
  • "The medication lifted the veil of confusion he had been living under." — Once medicated, things that had been foggy and unclear became sharp and understandable.

These fixed expressions with "veil" appear regularly in English and are worth knowing:

"To draw a veil over something" — To deliberately choose not to discuss or reveal something; to leave it in the past or keep it private. "She drew a veil over what had happened that night and never spoke of it again."

"Behind the veil" — On the hidden or unknown side of something. In a spiritual context, it often refers to what lies beyond death or beyond what humans can perceive — the unknown realm. "He believed his ancestors existed behind the veil."

"To lift the veil" (or "to raise the veil") — To reveal something that was previously hidden or secret; to expose the truth. "The documentary finally lifted the veil on the company's corrupt practices."

"To take the veil" — An old-fashioned expression meaning to become a nun (because a nun takes on the veil as part of her religious life).
The Emotional and Symbolic Weight of the Word

"Veil" is not a neutral word. It carries a sense of mystery, concealment, ceremony, and the unknown. Writers and speakers choose this word deliberately when they want to evoke that atmosphere. A "secret" is simply hidden. But something hidden behind a "veil" feels more ghostly, more elusive — something you sense is there, something you might almost make out, but can't quite grasp.

This is why the word appears so often in poetry, religious texts, and literary writing. It sits at the boundary between the known and the unknown, the seen and the unseen. That boundary — that in-between quality — is the soul of the word.

Whether literal (a piece of fabric over a bride's face) or figurative (a layer of secrecy hiding the truth), a veil always does the same fundamental thing: it partially conceals. It doesn't eliminate. It obscures, softens, and creates a sense of something being hidden just out of reach. That quality — of being there but not fully accessible — is what the word "veil" captures every single time it is used.
16998:
Before diving into the different meanings, it helps to know the idea that connects all of them:

A vein is a narrow channel, strip, or thread that runs through something larger — like a line running through a bigger body, usually carrying something or marking a distinct quality.

That one idea is the heart of every meaning below.
Meaning 1 — The One You've Probably Heard Of: Blood Vessels

In the human (or animal) body, a vein is a tube that carries blood back to the heart.

Your body has two types of blood vessels:

  • Arteries carry blood away from the heart to the rest of the body.
  • Veins bring that blood back to the heart.

Veins are the bluish-green lines you can sometimes see under the skin on your wrist or the back of your hand. They look blue not because the blood inside is blue (it's actually dark red when it has little oxygen), but because of how light passes through your skin.

"The doctor could easily see the veins in her forearm."
"He felt his pulse throbbing in a vein on his neck."

A key detail: veins have thinner, softer walls than arteries, because the blood inside them is under less pressure — it's travelling back to the heart, not being pushed out forcefully.
Meaning 2 — In Leaves and Insect Wings

If you hold a leaf up to the light, you'll see a network of thin lines running through it. Those lines are called veins.

In a leaf, veins are tiny tubes that carry water and nutrients from the stem into every part of the leaf, and they also carry food (made by the leaf through photosynthesis) back to the rest of the plant. They are essentially the leaf's internal supply lines.

"The skeleton of the dried leaf still showed all its veins clearly."
"Maple leaves have veins that branch out from the centre."

Similarly, the thin structural lines you see on an insect's wing (like a dragonfly's) are also called veins. They give the wing its shape and strength.
Meaning 3 — In Rock and the Earth (Geology and Mining)

In geology, a vein is a thin layer or streak of a mineral or metal running through surrounding rock. Think of it as a ribbon of one substance embedded inside a different one.

When miners look for gold, silver, copper, coal, or other valuable materials, they often find them in veins — narrow channels where the mineral has filled a crack in the rock over millions of years.

"They discovered a rich vein of gold deep inside the mountain."
"The miners followed the vein of coal further underground."

The vein can be just a few centimetres wide or several metres wide, and it can run for a short distance or stretch for kilometres.
Meaning 4 — A Streak or Thread of a Quality (Figurative)

This is a more abstract meaning, but it flows naturally from the geological sense above. When a quality, characteristic, or theme runs consistently through a piece of writing, a person's personality, or a creative work — the way a mineral vein runs through rock — we call it a vein.

"There is a vein of dark humour running through all of his novels."
"She noticed a vein of sadness beneath his cheerful manner."
"His poetry has a vein of mysticism in it."

Here, "vein" means: a quality that is not always on the surface but is consistently there, woven through the whole thing.
Meaning 5 — "In a ... vein" (A Particular Style or Mood)

This is a very common phrase. When someone says something is done "in a certain vein", they mean it is done in a particular style, spirit, or manner.

"He continued speaking in the same vein for another hour." (= in the same manner/tone)
"The film is made in a comedic vein." (= in a comic style)
"Let me offer something in a more serious vein." (= in a more serious manner)

Think of it this way: a "vein" of thought or style is like a channel you're flowing through. When you stay "in the same vein," you're continuing in the same channel.

Here is what ties every meaning of vein together:

ContextWhat the vein is
BodyA tube carrying blood through flesh
Leaf / WingA tube carrying nutrients through a flat surface
RockA strip of mineral running through stone
Writing / PersonalityA quality running through a larger whole
Speech / StyleA tone or manner running through what someone says or creates

Actually, let me say it in plain words instead:

In every case, a vein is something narrow that runs through something broader — whether it's a tube inside a body, a line inside a leaf, a stripe of gold inside rock, or a quality woven into a personality or a piece of writing. The word always suggests something that is embedded within, flowing through, or threading across a larger thing.

• "The marble floor had beautiful white veins running through it." (streaks of white mineral in stone)
  • "He has a strong vein of stubbornness in him." (a consistent quality in his character)
  • "The surgeon had to avoid the main vein during the operation." (blood vessel)
  • "In a similar vein, I'd like to add one more point." (in a similar manner/spirit)

That covers every dimension of the noun "vein" — biological, botanical, geological, figurative, and idiomatic. You now have the full picture.
16999:
You already know what a vein looks like — the thin, branching lines you see under your skin, in a leaf, or running through a slab of marble. When "vein" is used as a verb, it means to mark, streak, or run through something with lines that look exactly like those veins — thin, branching, thread-like patterns spreading across or through a surface or substance.

Think of it this way: a noun describes a thing; the verb form of that noun usually means "to do what that thing does" or "to make something look like that thing." So to vein something is to give it that characteristic branching-line appearance — or to run through it the way a vein does.

1. To mark something with vein-like lines (streaks, patterns)

This is the most common use. It means that thin, branching lines appear on or run through the surface of something — naturally or artificially.

"Cold air had veined her cheeks with red."
"The craftsman carefully veined the plaster to make it look like real marble."
"Frost veined the windowpane overnight."

Here, something (cold, a tool, frost) is creating vein-like lines on a surface. The subject is the thing doing the veining; the object is the thing being marked.

2. To run through something (like a vein runs through a body or rock)

Here, the subject itself is the thing acting like a vein — running through a larger substance in a thin, branching way.

"Quartz veins the granite throughout this mountain."
"Underground rivers vein the limestone beneath the valley."
"Gold veins the rock in this region."

This use is especially common in geology and geography. A mineral, water channel, or similar feature "veins" a rock or landscape when it runs through it in thin, spreading channels.

You'll very often see this verb in its past participle form — "veined" — used to describe a surface or material that has already been marked with these lines:

"veined marble" — marble with streaks running through it
"heavily veined leaves" — leaves with many visible lines branching across them
"blue-veined cheese" — cheese with blue or green mold running through it in vein-like streaks (think Gorgonzola or Stilton)
"a veined hand" — a hand where the veins are clearly visible under the skin

"Veined" simply means: marked or run through with veins or vein-like lines.
The Underlying Pattern (What Ties It All Together)

No matter the context, veining always involves thin lines spreading and branching through or across something — the way blood vessels branch under skin, the way cracks branch through stone, the way a river system fans out across a plain. The verb captures that specific visual: not just any mark, but a networked, branching, thread-like one.

This is why the word appears across so many domains — art and craft (faking marble), nature (leaves, skin, minerals), geology (ore deposits), and food (cheese). In every case, the same image applies: thin lines threading through a mass or across a surface.

• "Vein" as a verb is transitive — it takes an object. Something veins something else. ("Frost veined the glass." Not just "frost veined.")
  • It's not an everyday, high-frequency verb. You'll encounter it most in descriptive writing, nature writing, art, and geology.
  • "Veined" (past participle / adjective) is far more common than the active verb form in everyday use.

If you can visualize thin, branching lines threading through or across a surface — the way rivers look from above, the way cracks spread through glass, the way leaf veins radiate from a stem — you understand exactly what "to vein" means. The verb is simply describing the act of creating, or the state of having, that exact pattern.
